Supply-External Affairs Pensions and other benefits-
733. Pension to Miss Hilda L. Waddell, a former locally engaged employee, at an annual rate of 60,000 Brazilian cruzeiros, the equivalent in Canadian dollars for the balance of the present fiscal year being estimated at, $175.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to probe unduly because I see this item involves an individual. May we have the assurance of the minister that this is a normal and recurring type of obligation on the part of the government and it does not set a precedent of any kind?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this item relates to a provision made for a locally engaged employee at the Canadian embassy at Rio de Janeiro commencing December 1, 1958. The lady in question was employed as a telephone-receptionist at the embassy at a salary which translated into Canadian dollars, amounted to $864. She was 65 years of age and had completed a little more than nine years of employment with both the Department of External Affairs and the trade commissioner service in Rio de Janeiro. Since there is no pension system for local staffs abroad except in the United States and the United Kingdom it has been the policy of the treasury board to grant pensions on an ad hoc basis to deserving local employees.
It was reported to the board that the lady in question would be entitled upon retirement to a separation gratuity of one month's salary for each completed year of service, or $653 in Canadian currency. Payment of this amount would be in accordance with Brazilian labour law. I can go into more detail but I think that is enough to indicate to my hon. friend the nature of the item.

I was just doing to indicate to the Minister of Finance that my curiosity arose from the fact that reference was made in the report of the Auditor General for the year ending March 31, 1958 to a practice which he said was contrary to the statutes with respect to paying pensions even, I think, in the United Kingdom and United States to employees of Canada engaged outside of Canada. Has the government some plan of regularizing that practice which was criticized in the report?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, our view is that this is a practice that is properly authorized by statute of this parliament.

I think there has been some practice which the Auditor General has pointed to but I believe he said it ran directly counter to a specific prohibition in our basic pension statute. I know that this is in effect legislating for a specific item. My question was whether or not the minister had been

Supply-External Affairs giving consideration to our practice as criticized by the Auditor General even in the United Kingdom and the United States and whether or not he proposes to bring in some legislation to regularize what was criticized.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Those papers are not here, Mr. Chairman. We can have a look at them another time.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Terminable Services-
734. Purchase of flour to be given to the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East,-Further amount required and, notwithstanding section 35 of the Financial Administration Act, to authorize payments to be made pursuant to this vote up to the 1st day of April, 1960, $1,500,000.

Mr. Chairman, I have been wondering about this item and item No. 741 which is for the purchase of wheat and flour to be given to commonwealth countries in south and southeast Asia. The passing of this item will enable the government to give this assistance in the coming fiscal year which concludes on April 1, 1960. My question is this. Why should we not vote the money for the amounts of wheat delivered in the next fiscal year and only vote at this time what has been delivered in this fiscal year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the purpose is to enable this flour to be moved as quickly as possible. Some of it is moving before March 31. It is moving as fast as the Minister of Trade and Commerce can arrange for its movement. This particular item of $1,500,000 under item No. 734 was announced
in the house by the late secretary of state for external affairs within the last fortnight. The purpose of providing this item now on a non-lapsing basis as of March 31, 1959 is to enable the government to move this wheat as quickly as possible. You cannot just cut off a movement at March 31 midnight. This is the proper, and I think I may say the businesslike way, of making provision of this kind. It comes before parliament. Parliament has full view of the matter. This makes it possible to move this flour as quickly as opportunity is afforded.

This is a large sum and while we do not want to hold up this amount it occurs to me we could between now and March 31 vote for that portion of the flour or wheat that has been sent up to that period. Why should not the major part of this be left over until next year?
